unable.e: From Middle English unable, unabel, unhable, unhabil, equivalent to un- + able.
unable.g: Not able; lacking a certain ability.

unable.e: From Middle English unablen, equivalent to un- + able.

unacceptable.e: From Middle English unacceptabylle, equivalent to un- + acceptable.

unaccustom.g: To make or become used to a change from something one was accustomed to.

unanswered.e: From Middle English unansuered, unanswerd, equivalent to un- + answered.
unanswered.g: That has not been answered or addressed.

unavoidable.e: From Middle English unavoidable, equivalent to un- + avoidable.
unavoidable.g: Impossible to avoid; bound to happen.

unbelief.e: From Middle English unbilefe, unbileve, equivalent to un- + belief.
unbelief.g: An absence (or rejection) of belief, especially religious belief.

unbeliever.e: From un- + believer, perhaps a corruption of earlier wanbeliever (“unbeliever”).
unbeliever.g: One who does not believe, particularly in a deity (used by believers to describe people who do not believe in the same deity or deities as t

unborn.e: From Middle English unborn, from Old English unboren, from Proto-Germanic *unburanaz. Equivalent to un- + born.
unborn.g: Not yet born; yet to come; future.

unbury.e: From Middle English unburien, unbirien, from Old English *unbyrġan (compare Old English unbyrġed (“unburied”)), equivalent to un- + bury.
unbury.g: To dig up, to remove from the ground.

uncertain.e: From Middle English uncerteyn. By surface analysis, un- + certain.

uncertainly.e: From Middle English uncerteynliche, uncertanlye. By surface analysis, uncertain + -ly or un- + certainly.

uncertainty.e: From Middle English uncerteynte; equivalent to un- + certainty or uncertain + -ty.
uncertainty.g: Doubt; the condition of being uncertain or without conviction.

unchange.g: To revert or reverse a change

unchangeable.e: From Middle English unchaungeable; equivalent to un- + changeable.
unchangeable.g: Not changeable; incapable of being changed or of changing; immutable.

uncircumcised.e: From Middle English uncircumcised, equivalent to un- + circumcised. Subsidiary definitions are much influenced by traditions of the Abrahamic religions.

uncircumcision.g: The absence of a circumcision; not being circumcised.

uncle.e: From Middle English uncle, borrowed from Anglo-Norman uncle and Old French oncle, from Vulgar Latin *aunclum, from Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”, literally “little grandfather”).
uncle.g: The brother or brother-in-law of one’s parent.

unclean.e: From Middle English unclene, from Old English unclǣne, equivalent to un- + clean.

uncleanness.e: From Middle English unclennesse, from Old English unclǣnnes; equivalent to unclean + -ness.

unclothe.e: From Middle English unclothen, equivalent to un- + clothe.
unclothe.g: To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked.

uncomely.e: From Middle English uncomli, uncomelich, uncumelich, unkumelich, equivalent to un- + comely.
From Middle English uncomly, uncomli, from the adjective (see above).
uncomely.g: In an uncomely way; inappropriately, unappealingly.

unconcerned.g: Indifferent and having no interest; aloof.

uncover.e: From Middle English uncoveren, equivalent to un- + cover.

unction.e: Blend of unc (“older man”) + function (“social occasion”)

uncut.e: From Middle English unkut, uncutte, unkyt, unkutt, equivalent to un- + cut.

under.e: From Middle English under, from Old English under, from Proto-West Germanic *undar, from Proto-Germanic *under, from a merger of Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér (“under”) and *h₁entér (“inside”).
under.g: Beneath; below; at or to the bottom of, or the area covered or surmounted by.

undercut.e: From Middle English undercutten, equivalent to under- + cut.
undercut.g: A cut made in the lower part of something; the material so removed.

underfoot.e: From Middle English underfoote, underfote, equivalent to under- + foot.
underfoot.g: Situated under one's foot or feet.

undergarment.g: Any garment worn underneath others, especially one worn next to the skin; an item of underwear.

undergo.e: From Middle English undergon, from Old English undergān (“to undergo, undermine, ruin”), equivalent to under- + go.
undergo.g: To experience; to pass through a phase.

underneath.e: From Middle English undernethe, undernethen, from Old English underneoþan (“underneath”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *underniþer. Equivalent to under- + neath.

undersetter.g: One who, or that which, undersets or supports; a prop; a support; a pedestal.

understand.e: From Middle English understanden, from Old English understandan (“to understand”), from Proto-West Germanic *understandan (“to stand between, understand”), from Proto-Germanic *understandaną (“to stand between, understand”), equivalent to Old English under- (“between, inter-”) + standan (“to stand”) (Modern English under- + stand).
understand.g: To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.

understanding.e: From Middle English understandyng, understondynge, understondinde, undirstondend, understandande, from Old English understandende, from Proto-West Germanic *undarstandandī.
understanding.g: Showing compassion, tolerance, and forbearance; sympathetically aware.

undertake.e: From Middle English undertaken; equivalent to under- + take (after undernim).
undertake.g: To take upon oneself; to start, to embark on.

underway.e: Calque of Dutch onderweg (“underway”), equivalent to under- + way.
underway.g: In motion, in progress; being done or carried out; on a journey.
A road, track, path, or street for going under another way or obstacle; an underpass.

undo.e: From Middle English undōn, from Old English ondōn, from Proto-West Germanic *andadōn (“to undo”), equivalent to un- + do.
undo.g: To reverse the effects of an action.

undone.e: From Middle English undon, from Old English ondōn, from Proto-Germanic *andadōnaz, past participle of *andadōną (“to undo”), equivalent to undo + -en (past participle ending).

undressed.g: Having partially or completely removed one's clothes.

unease.e: From Middle English unese, equivalent to un- + ease.
unease.g: Trouble; misery; a feeling of disquiet or concern.

unease.e: From Middle English unesen, equivalent to un- + ease.

unequal.e: From Middle English unequale, equivalent to un- + equal.

uneven.e: From Middle English uneven, from Old English unefen (“unequal, unlike, dissimilar, diverse, irregular”), equivalent to un- + even.
uneven.g: Of a surface, not even; covered with raised spots, pits and grooves.

unfair.e: From Middle English unfair (“unattractive, unseemly”), from Old English unfæġer (“ugly”), equivalent to un- + fair.

unfaithful.e: From Middle English unfeithful, equivalent to un- + faithful.

unfold.e: From Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan (“to unfold”), equivalent to un- + fold.
From un- + fold (“to confine into a fold or pen”).
unfold.g: To release from a fold or pen.

unforgive.g: To revoke or rescind forgiveness of.

unfruitful.e: From Middle English unfruytful; equivalent to un- + fruitful.

unfruitfulness.g: the state or property of being unfruitful; fruitlessness, barrenness

ungird.e: From un- + gird; or possibly continuing Middle English ungirden, ungurden, from Old English ungyrdan (“to ungird”).
ungird.g: To loosen or remove the girdle or band of.

ungodly.e: From Middle English ungodli, from un- (prefix meaning ‘not’), + godli (“belonging to God; resembling God, godlike”). Godli is derived from Old English godlīċ (“divine, godlike; godly”), from god (“god”) + -līċ (“suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘characteristic of, pertaining to’”).
ungodly.g: Of a person: lacking reverence for God; of an action: not in accordance with God's will or religious teachings.

ungodly.e: From Middle English ungodli (“cruelly, maliciously, wickedly; unfairly, unlawfully, wrongly; discourteously, rudely”), from un- (prefix meaning ‘not’), + godli (“excellently; pleasingly, splendidly; courteously, graciously; gladly, willingly; righteously; properly, rightly; at all, possibly; much”).
ungodly.g: In an impious, irreverent, or ungodly manner; ungodlily.

unholy.e: From Middle English unholi, unhaliȝ, from Old English unhāliġ, from Proto-Germanic *unhailagaz, equivalent to un- + holy.
unholy.g: Not holy; (by extension) evil, impure, or otherwise perverted.

unicorn.e: From Middle English unicorne, unikorn, from Anglo-Norman unicorne, Old French unicorne, and their source, Latin ūnicornis, (from ūnus (“one”) + cornū (“horn”)), a calque of Ancient Greek μονόκερως (monókerōs, “having one horn”, (from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”))).
unicorn.g: A mythical horselike creature with a horn on its forehead, supposed to be extremely rare and to be drawn to virgins and other chaste maidens

unintentionally.g: Without meaning to, in an unintentional manner, not intentionally.

union.e: From Middle English unyoun, from Old French union, from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”).
union.g: The act of uniting or joining two or more things into one.

unique.e: Borrowed from French unique, from Latin unicus.
unique.g: Being the only one of its kind; unequaled, unparalleled or unmatched.

unison.e: From Middle English unisoun, from Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus (“having the same sound”), from ūni- + sonus (“sound”).
unison.g: Identical pitch between two notes or sounds; the simultaneous playing of notes of identical pitch (or separated by one or more octaves).

unit.e: Formerly unite, a later form of unity; see unity.
unit.g: Oneness, singularity, seen as a component of a whole number; a magnitude of one.

unite.e: From Middle English uniten, from Latin ūnītus, perfect passive participle of ūniō.

unity.e: From Middle English unite, from Anglo-Norman, Old French unité, from Latin ūnitās, from ūnus (“one”) + noun of state suffix -itās, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one, single”), hence distantly related to one and an. By surface analysis, unite + -y.
unity.g: Oneness: the state or fact of being one undivided entity.

universe.e: From Middle English universe, from Old French univers, from Latin universum (“all things, as a whole, the universe”), neuter of universus (“all together, whole, entire, collective, general, literally turned or combined into one”), from uni-, combining form of unus (“one”) + versus (“turned”), perfect passive participle of vertō (“to turn”).
universe.g: The sum of everything that exists in the cosmos.

unknown.e: From Middle English *unknowen, *uniknowen, uniknowe, from Old English unġecnāwen (“unknown”), equivalent to un- + known.
unknown.g: Not known; unidentified; not well known.

unlawful.e: From Middle English unlawful; equivalent to un- + lawful.
unlawful.g: Prohibited; not permitted by law (either civil or criminal law; see illegal)

unlearned.e: From Middle English unlernyd (“obliterated from memory, forgotten”), equivalent to unlearn + -ed.

unleavened.g: Without any yeast or other raising agent.

unless.e: From Middle English unlesse, earlier on lesse (modern on + less), from (not) on lesse (than) (“(not) on a less compelling condition (than)”). The quality of negation in the word and the lack of stress changed on to un-.
unless.g: Except on a specified condition; if not.

unlike.e: From Middle English unlic, unlich, from Old English unlīċ, unġelīċ (“unlike, different, dissimilar, diverse”), from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, un- + like.
unlike.g: Not like; dissimilar (to); having no resemblance; unalike.

unlike.e: From Middle English unliken, unlyken, equivalent to un- + like.

unloose.e: From Middle English unlosen (“to loosen, untie; to uncover, unwrap; to extend; to free, liberate, release; to disengage; to detach oneself; to make (someone) weak; to abolish; to destroy”), from un- (intensifying prefix) + losen (“to free, let loose, release; to loosen, untie; to come undone or unfastened; to open; to relax; to remove; to melt; to resolve.
unloose.g: To loosen or undo (something that entangles, fastens, holds, or interlocks).

unlove.g: The lack, absence, or omission of love; lovelessness; enmity; neglect; hate.

unlove.e: From Middle English unloven, equivalent to un- (reversal prefix) + love (verb).
unlove.g: To lose one's love (for someone or something).

unmerciful.e: From Middle English unmerciful, unmercifull; equivalent to un- + merciful.

unmindful.e: From Middle English unmyndefull; equivalent to un- + mindful.

unnatural.e: From Middle English unnatural, unnaturel, equivalent to un- + natural.

unoccupied.e: From Middle English unoccupied; equivalent to un- + occupied.
unoccupied.g: Not inhabited, especially by a tenant

unpleasant.e: From Middle English unplesaunt, equivalent to un- + pleasant.

unpleasing.e: From Middle English un-plesyng, equivalent to un- + pleasing.

unreasonable.e: From Middle English unresonable, equivalent to un- + reasonable, originally partly after Latin irratiōnābilis.
unreasonable.g: Without the ability to reason; unreasoning.

unrest.e: From Middle English unreste, equivalent to un- + rest.
unrest.g: A state of trouble, confusion and turbulence, especially in a political context; a time of riots, demonstrations and protests.

unrighteous.e: From Middle English unrightwis, from Old English unrihtwīs; equivalent to un- + righteous.

unrighteousness.e: From Middle English unriȝtwisnesse, from Old English unrihtwīsnes; equivalent to un- + righteousness or unrighteous + -ness.

unripe.e: From Old English unrīpe. Equivalent to un- + ripe.

unruly.e: From Middle English unruly (“unquiet, restless”), equivalent to un- + rule + -ly (compare Middle English ruly, reuli (“subject to a religious rule, regular”)), but also representing a modified continuation of earlier Middle English unrouly, unroly (“unquiet, restless”), equivalent to un- + roolie.

unscathed.e: A calque of Middle Scots unskaithit, from Early Scots unscathit; by surface analysis, un- + scathed.
unscathed.g: Not harmed or damaged in any way; untouched.

unschool.g: To educate (a child) in an alternative to the regular school method, focused on the learner-chosen activities as a primary means for learnin

unsearchable.e: From Middle English unserchable, equivalent to un- + searchable.
unsearchable.g: That cannot be searched or investigated into; inscrutable, unknowable.

unseemly.e: From Middle English unsemli, probably a partial calque of Old Norse úsǽmiligr (“unseemly”); equivalent to un- + seemly.
unseemly.g: Inconsistent with established standards of good form or taste.

unseen.e: From Middle English unsen, unseyn, unseien, from Old English unġesewen, from Proto-Germanic *unsewanaz, equivalent to un- + seen.

unshod.e: From Middle English unshod, unschod from Old English unsċōd, equivalent to un- + shod.

unspeakable.e: From Middle English unspekable, equivalent to un- + speakable.
unspeakable.g: Incapable of being spoken or uttered.

unstable.e: From Middle English unstable; equivalent to un- (“not”) + stable. Piecewise doublet of instable and astable.

unstable.g: To release (an animal) from a stable.

unstop.e: From Middle English unstoppen, equivalent to un- + stop.
unstop.g: To remove a stoppage; to clear a blockage.

unstrung.g: Not strung; having had the strings undone or removed.

unsuccessfully.g: Not successfully; without success; to no avail.

untaken.e: From Middle English untaken; equivalent to un- + taken.

unthankful.e: From Middle English unthankful, from Old English unþancful, unþancfull, unġeþancfull (“unthankful, ungrateful”), equivalent to un- + thankful.

untie.e: From Middle English untien, unteyen, untyȝen, untiȝen, from Old English untīġan (“to untie”), equivalent to un- + tie.
untie.g: To loosen, as something interlaced or knotted; to disengage the parts of.

until.e: From Middle English vntil, until, untill, ontil, ontill, perhaps representing a northern variant of Middle English unto (see Modern English unto). By surface analysis, un- (“against; toward; up to”) + till.
until.g: Up to the time of (something happening); pending.

untimely.e: From Middle English untymely (also earlier untimliche), equivalent to un- + timely.

untrouble.g: To free from trouble or disturbance.

untrue.e: From Middle English untrewe, from Old English untrīewe, from Proto-West Germanic *untriuwī, from Proto-Germanic *untriwwiz. Equivalent to un- + true.

unveiled.e: From Middle English unveiled, vnueylyd, equivalent to un- + veil + -ed.
unveiled.g: Not wearing, or not covered by, a veil.

unwalled.e: From Middle English unwalled, unwallyd; equivalent to un- + walled.

unwashed.e: From Middle English unwasched, unwasschyd, unwessched, a weak verb conjugation of earlier Middle English unwaschen (“unwashen”), equivalent to un- + washed.

unwashen.e: From Middle English unwaschen, from Old English unwæsċen (“not washed”), equivalent to un- + washen.

unwholesome.e: From Middle English unholsom; equivalent to un- + wholesome.
unwholesome.g: Not wholesome; unfavorable to health; unhealthful.

unwise.e: From Middle English unwis, from Old English unwīs (“unwise, foolish, ignorant, uninformed, insane”), equivalent to un- + wise.

unwittingly.e: From Middle English on-wytyngly, un-wetandly, unweteynglye, unwetinglie, un-wetinglye, unwetyngly, unwitandly, unwitendely, unwitingly, unwittandly, unwityngli, unwityngly, unwytyngeleche, unwytyngli, equivalent to unwitting + -ly or un- + wittingly.
unwittingly.g: In an unwitting manner; inadvertently, obliviously, unintentionally, unknowingly.

unworthy.e: From Middle English unworthy, equivalent to un- + worthy.
unworthy.g: Not worthy; lacking value or merit; worthless.
